rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results and discussion <U+2013> the authors develop their own software, run 600 randomly generated hydrant configurations for the Sinistra Ofanto district at 1,200 and 600 l/s, conduct laboratory tests of hydrant flow regulators (Fig. 3) and indoor sprinkler pattern tests (Fig. 4), and optimise four designs of one on-farm sector with Labye's method (Figs. 8-10).
rows.notes: The study does not compare the investment cost of on-demand collective networks with any other delivery arrangement, nor does it attribute a higher cost of on-demand networks to guaranteeing peak-period supply. What it shows is a simulated cost-reliability trade-off for the on-farm sprinkler network supplied by one hydrant: the design for low hydrant pressure (D24, large pipes) is 38% more expensive than D34 but never fails across the 24-65 m hydrant pressure range, while cheaper small-pipe designs (D49, D55) fail with high probability at peak demand (Results; Figs. 8, 10). This is a design-optimisation and hydraulic simulation result for the on-farm network; the pressure-probability and cost outputs are not checked against measurements from the real system (only component-level lab curves are used as inputs). The authors themselves state the results are very specific to the case study and that wind and non-pipe costs were neglected. Hence no own evidence on the claim as worded.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a modelling/case-study paper on how on-demand distribution-system pressure fluctuations affect on-farm sprinkler network design and performance in an Italian district; it is cited here for a claim about the investment cost of on-demand networks, which it addresses only indirectly through on-farm pipe-cost versus failure-risk simulations.
